name: Heat capacity
kicker: Heat needed to warm something one degree · Why water heats up so slowly
dates: Studied by Joseph Black in the 1760s
briefing: Heat capacity tells how much heat it takes to warm something up by one degree. Water’s value is unusually high, which is why a pot of water takes a while to boil, beach sand gets hot long before the ocean does, and coastal towns have milder weather than places far inland. Scientists often compare substances by their specific heat, the heat capacity of just one gram, and water’s is about 4.18 joules per gram per degree Celsius.
answerHtml: Heat capacity (accept specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity, or thermal capacity; prompt on C; do not accept “latent heat”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The “lambda point” of helium, near 2.2 kelvins, is named for the Greek-letter shape that a graph of this quantity makes as helium turns into a superfluid. A metal’s value of this quantity jumps suddenly at the temperature where the metal becomes a superconductor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: In 1819, Pierre Louis Dulong [“doo-LONG”] and Alexis Petit [“puh-TEE”] found that many solid elements have nearly the same value of this quantity per mole of atoms, about 25 joules per kelvin. Diamond’s value is far lower than that rule predicts at room temperature.
tossups.r: Water has an unusually high value of it. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in joules per kelvin, which tells how much heat it takes to warm something up.

tossups.p: Stars and black holes have negative values of this quantity, meaning they actually get hotter as they lose energy. Unlike its “specific” version, the ordinary version of this quantity depends on how much material an object contains. A full swimming pool has a far larger value of it than a cup of water.
tossups.r: Water has an unusually high value of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Sea breezes blow onshore on sunny afternoons partly because land has a lower value of this quantity than the ocean, so the land warms up faster. Coastal towns have milder summers and winters than inland towns because of water’s high value of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise something’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Students can find a metal’s value of this quantity per gram by dropping a hot sample into water inside a coffee-cup calorimeter and measuring how much the water warms. The formula Q equals m c delta T uses that per-gram value, symbolized lowercase c.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which is unusually high for water and tells how much heat it takes to warm something up.

tossups.p: The food “Calorie” on nutrition labels is really a kilocalorie, and the original small calorie was chosen so that water’s value of this quantity per gram came out to exactly one. In joules, that per-gram value for water is about 4.18 per degree Celsius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Car engines are cooled with water-based coolant because water’s high value of this quantity lets it soak up a lot of heat while warming only a little. Water’s high value of this quantity comes from the energy needed to break its hydrogen bonds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in joules per kelvin, that tells how much heat it takes to warm something by one degree.

tossups.p: The speed of sound in a gas depends on the ratio of this quantity measured at constant pressure to this quantity measured at constant volume, a ratio called gamma. For a gas, the constant-pressure value of this quantity is always the larger one, because some of the added heat goes into pushing the gas outward.
tossups.r: Water has a high value of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: On a heating curve, the slanted sections are less steep when a substance has a larger value of this quantity, while the flat sections show latent heat being absorbed during melting and boiling. Metals like copper have low values of this quantity, so they heat up quickly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which is unusually high for water and is measured in joules per kelvin.

tossups.p: Before using a calorimeter to measure a reaction, chemists find the calorimeter’s own value of this quantity, often called its “calorimeter constant.” Multiplying an object’s value of this quantity by its temperature change gives the heat it gained or lost.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: In the 1760s, the Scottish chemist Joseph Black studied this quantity, and he also discovered latent heat. Black showed that equal masses of different substances need different amounts of heat to warm by the same number of degrees.
tossups.r: Water’s per-gram value of it is about 4.18 joules per degree Celsius. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is especially high for water.

tossups.p: Nitrogen gas has a larger value of this quantity per mole than argon does, because nitrogen’s two-atom molecules can also store energy by spinning. Helium and argon, both made of single atoms, have the same value of this quantity per mole.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

tossups.p: Thick adobe or stone walls have a large value of this quantity, so they keep desert homes cool during the hot day and warm through the cold night. Oceans store huge amounts of heat because of water’s large value of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in joules per kelvin, which explains why beach sand heats up faster than the ocean.

tossups.p: Albert Einstein’s 1907 model of a solid treated its atoms as tiny vibrating springs to explain why this quantity shrinks at very low temperatures, and Peter Debye [“duh-BYE”] improved that model in 1912. Both models used the new quantum ideas of Max Planck.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the amount of heat needed to warm an object by one degree.

tossups.p: Per gram, ice has only about half the value of this quantity that liquid water has, and steam also has about half of liquid water’s value. Builders use the term “thermal mass” for a large value of this quantity in materials like concrete and brick.
tossups.r: Its per-gram form is called “specific.” For 10 points, name this quantity, the heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree.

clues.t: The amount of heat needed to raise an object’s temperature by one degree
Its “specific” version is per unit mass (per gram or kilogram); its “molar” version is per mole
Water’s value is unusually high: about 4.18 joules (1 calorie) per gram per degree Celsius
Explains why beach sand gets hot long before the ocean does
Measured in joules per kelvin; the per-mass version in joules per kilogram per kelvin (or joules per gram per degree Celsius)
Q = m c ΔT: heat equals mass times the per-gram value (lowercase c) times the temperature change
Measured with a calorimeter, like a coffee-cup calorimeter; a calorimeter’s own value is its “calorimeter constant”
Land’s lower value lets it warm faster than the sea, helping cause afternoon sea breezes and milder coastal climates
Metals like copper and iron have low values (copper’s per gram is less than a tenth of water’s), so they heat up fast
Depends on how much material there is: a swimming pool’s value is far larger than a cup of water’s
On a heating curve, a larger value makes the slanted sections less steep; the flat sections show latent heat
Water’s high value, from its hydrogen bonds, makes it a good coolant for car engines
Helium’s “lambda point,” near 2.2 K, is named for the λ shape its graph makes as helium becomes a superfluid
Dulong and Petit (1819): many solid elements have about 25 joules per kelvin per mole of atoms
Einstein’s 1907 model of vibrating atoms and Debye’s 1912 model explain why it drops toward zero for cold solids
Diamond’s value at room temperature is far below what the Dulong–Petit rule predicts
Stars and black holes have negative values: they get hotter as they lose energy
Scottish chemist Joseph Black studied it in the 1760s, showing that equal masses of different substances need different amounts of heat to warm equally; he also discovered latent heat
The constant-pressure value divided by the constant-volume value is gamma, which helps set the speed of sound in a gas
For a gas, the constant-pressure value is larger than the constant-volume value, since some heat goes into pushing the gas outward
Nitrogen gas has a larger value per mole than argon, because its two-atom molecules can also store energy by spinning; single-atom helium and argon share the same value per mole
A metal’s value jumps suddenly at the temperature where it becomes a superconductor
Per gram, ice and steam each have only about half of liquid water’s value
Builders call a large value “thermal mass”: thick adobe or stone walls keep desert homes cool by day and warm at night
The original small calorie was chosen so that water’s per-gram value is exactly 1 calorie per degree Celsius; a food Calorie is really a kilocalorie

trap.title: Not latent heat
trap.body: Heat capacity tells how much heat it takes to change an object’s temperature. Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a phase change, like melting or boiling, while the temperature does not change at all. Players also blurt out “temperature,” and some questions want only the “specific” version per gram, called specific heat, which is accepted here.
trap.fix: Warming by one degree, joules per kelvin, Q = m c ΔT, water’s 4.18, sea breezes, and calorimeters point to heat capacity or specific heat. Melting or boiling at a steady temperature, the flat parts of a heating curve, and heats of fusion or vaporization point to latent heat.
trap.line: Real answer line: Heat capacity (accept specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity, or thermal capacity; prompt on C; do not accept “latent heat”)
